cards.front: Radiant energy is energy carried by {{c1::light}}.
cards.quote: Radiant energy is energy carried by light.
cards.section: One leaf cell, two energy jobs

cards.front: In a green leaf cell, which organelle carries out photosynthesis?
cards.back: The chloroplast, a green part of the cell that takes in light.
cards.quote: It happens in a chloroplast, a green part of the cell that takes in light.
cards.section: One leaf cell, two energy jobs

cards.front: Which organelle does most of cellular respiration, and which kinds of cells have it?
cards.back: The mitochondrion. It is found in almost all plant and animal cells.
cards.quote: Most of it happens in mitochondria, small parts found in almost all plant and animal cells.
cards.section: One leaf cell, two energy jobs

cards.front: Cell parts like chloroplasts and mitochondria are called {{c1::organelles}}.
cards.quote: Cell parts like these are called organelles.
cards.section: One leaf cell, two energy jobs

cards.front: Which process adds oxygen in light, and which process uses oxygen day and night?
cards.back: Photosynthesis adds oxygen in light. Cellular respiration uses oxygen day and night.
cards.quote: The one idea: Photosynthesis adds oxygen in light; respiration uses oxygen day and night.
cards.section: What one process makes, the other can use

cards.front: What is a reactant, and what is a product?
cards.back: A reactant goes into a chemical process. A product comes out of it.
cards.quote: A reactant is a substance that goes into a chemical process. A product is a substance that comes out.
cards.section: What one process makes, the other can use

cards.front: Does warm water or cold water hold more dissolved oxygen?
cards.back: Cold water holds more. Warm water holds less oxygen than cold water.
cards.quote: Warm water holds less oxygen than cold water.
cards.section: Why a real creek is bumpier than the model

cards.front: Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
cards.back: carbon dioxide + water + radiant energy → sugar (glucose) + oxygen
cards.quote: Photosynthesis uses it to make sugar (glucose) and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water.
cards.section: One leaf cell, two energy jobs

cards.front: Write the word equation for cellular respiration.
cards.back: sugar (glucose) + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy for the cell
cards.quote: Cellular respiration joins sugar with oxygen and releases energy the cell can use.
cards.section: One leaf cell, two energy jobs

cards.front: Why are photosynthesis and cellular respiration called interdependent, even though they happen in different organelles?
cards.back: The products of either process can supply reactants for the other: sugar and oxygen feed respiration, and carbon dioxide and water feed photosynthesis.
cards.quote: Check the table: the products of either process can supply reactants for the other.
cards.section: What one process makes, the other can use

cards.front: Can carbon, oxygen and hydrogen atoms be reused through these processes? Can energy?
cards.back: Matter can be used again, many times. Energy flows one way: it changes form, from light to chemical energy in sugar to energy for life processes and heat.
cards.quote: Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen atoms can move through these processes many times, even while matter enters or leaves a cell or creek.
cards.section: What one process makes, the other can use

cards.front: Why does a green leaf cell respire day and night but make new sugar only in light?
cards.back: Respiration uses sugar and oxygen and needs no light. Photosynthesis needs radiant energy, so it runs only in light.
cards.quote: Key idea: A green leaf cell makes sugar in its chloroplasts and releases energy from sugar in its mitochondria.
cards.section: One leaf cell, two energy jobs

cards.front: In the simple creek model, when does dissolved oxygen rise, and when does it fall?
cards.back: It rises when photosynthesis adds oxygen faster than respiration uses it. It falls when respiration uses oxygen faster.
cards.quote: Key idea: In the simple creek model, oxygen rises when photosynthesis adds it faster than respiration uses it, and falls when respiration uses it faster.
cards.section: Why a real creek is bumpier than the model

cards.front: Name two nonliving things that can change the oxygen a sensor measures in a real creek.
cards.back: Tides bring different water past the sensor. Air can add oxygen at the surface or take some away when the water holds extra. Temperature also matters.
cards.quote: Tides bring different water past a sensor. Air can add oxygen at the surface or take some away when the water holds extra.
cards.section: Why a real creek is bumpier than the model

cards.front: A root cell receives sugar from a leaf. Which process can it run, and which organelle does most of that work?
cards.back: Cellular respiration, mostly in its mitochondria. Without chloroplasts, it does not photosynthesize.
cards.quote: A root cell receives sugar from a leaf. Which process can it run, and which organelle does most of that work?
cards.section: One leaf cell, two energy jobs

cards.front: A snail and a water plant share a sealed jar of water on a sunny windowsill. What does the snail give off that the plant can use in photosynthesis?
cards.back: Carbon dioxide. The snail's cells respire and give off carbon dioxide, a reactant of photosynthesis.
cards.quote: Check the table: the products of either process can supply reactants for the other.
cards.section: What one process makes, the other can use

cards.front: In a virtual Bay tank, you switch the same tank from sunny to cloudy. How does its noon oxygen compare?
cards.back: Noon oxygen is lower. With less light, photosynthesis adds oxygen more slowly, while respiration continues.
cards.quote: With less light, photosynthesis adds oxygen more slowly, while respiration continues.
cards.section: Explore: run a day and a night in a Bay tank

cards.front: In a virtual Bay tank, you add many fish and remove most of the grass. What happens to oxygen by dawn?
cards.back: Dawn oxygen is lower. More animals use oxygen, while less grass is there to add it in light.
cards.quote: More animals use oxygen, while less grass is there to add it in light.
cards.section: Explore: run a day and a night in a Bay tank

cards.front: At Taskinas Creek, dissolved oxygen was 10.7 mg/L at 6 p.m. and 6.4 mg/L the next midnight, with no light after dark. How much did oxygen change, and what best explains it?
cards.back: It fell by 4.3 mg/L (10.7 minus 6.4). With no light, photosynthesis added no oxygen, while living things kept respiring.
cards.quote: How much did oxygen fall between 6 p.m. and midnight? What was the light during most of that time?
cards.section: Evidence: a real day in Taskinas Creek

cards.front: In the Taskinas Creek table, oxygen was lowest (4.0 mg/L) at 6 a.m. and highest (10.7 mg/L) at 6 p.m. How much light was there at each time, and what does that show?
cards.back: Light in the 15 minutes before each reading was about 90.8 at 6 a.m. and 240.6 at 6 p.m., both mmol photons per m2. Oxygen was lowest after a night of respiration and highest after a day of photosynthesis.
cards.quote: Find the lowest and highest oxygen in the table. Was it light or dark at each time?
cards.section: Evidence: a real day in Taskinas Creek

cards.front: In Taskinas Creek, oxygen fell from 5.7 to 4.6 mg/L between noon and 3 p.m. in bright light, and the water warmed only about 1 °C. Is temperature the best explanation?
cards.back: No. The water warmed only about 1 °C, too little to explain the dip. Another nonliving process, such as tide or air exchange, could help explain it.
cards.quote: The water warmed only about 1 °C, too little to explain the dip.
cards.section: Why temperature does not explain the 3 p.m. dip

cards.front: At Taskinas Creek, oxygen jumped from 4.7 to 9.5 mg/L in 15 minutes soon after the tide turned and flowed in. Why is this unlikely to be local photosynthesis alone?
cards.back: Photosynthesis cannot add that much that fast in one spot. The tide most likely carried in water that already held extra oxygen made elsewhere.
cards.quote: Photosynthesis cannot add that much that fast in one spot.
cards.section: The sudden jump

cards.front: You test whether a water plant adds oxygen in light and uses it in dark. Besides jars with plants, what jars do you need, and why?
cards.back: Control jars of water with no plant, in light and in dark. They show how oxygen changes without the plant, so any extra change in the plant jars can be credited to the plant.
cards.quote: Control: jars with water and no plant, in light and dark. They show how oxygen changes without the plant.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A student says the sudden oxygen jump from the tide shows the photosynthesis and respiration model is wrong. How do you reply?
cards.back: The model is not wrong. Photosynthesis explains where new oxygen is made, and respiration explains where living things use it. The tide changes when oxygen reaches the sensor.
cards.quote: None of this makes the cell model wrong. Photosynthesis explains where new oxygen is made, and respiration explains where living things use it.
cards.section: The sudden jump
